item.title: What Sleep Does for Your Memory
item.summary: An explainer on how sleep helps the brain keep what we learn, and why staying up all night before an exam often backfires.
item.content_markdown:
It is two in the morning before an important exam, and Madina is still at her desk, surrounded by notes and empty cups of tea. Like many students, she believes that every extra hour of revision will earn her extra marks. Sleep, in her view, is time she simply cannot afford. Scientists who study memory would probably tell her that she has it the wrong way round.

## Learning happens twice

When we learn something new, the brain forms a memory that is still fragile. Over the following hours, that memory has to be stabilised, a process researchers call consolidation. A large body of research suggests that much of this work takes place while we sleep. In other words, learning seems to happen twice: once when we read or practise, and again at night, when the brain quietly sorts and strengthens what it has taken in.

During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay recent experiences, helping to move important information into longer-term storage. Other stages of sleep are thought to help us connect new knowledge with what we already know, which may be why a problem that seemed impossible in the evening sometimes looks simpler in the morning.

## The cost of an all-nighter

If sleep helps to fix memories, then skipping it has a price. After a night without sleep, most people find it harder to concentrate, slower to react and more likely to make careless mistakes. The material Madina studies at two in the morning may never be properly stored, and the tiredness she carries into the exam room can make it harder to recall even the things she learned weeks ago.

This does not mean that sleep can replace studying. A brain cannot consolidate information that was never learned in the first place. The point is that the two work together.

## Practical lessons

What can learners do with this knowledge? First, it is usually more effective to spread revision over several days, so that each night of sleep has something to work on. Second, a short review of key points before bed may help, as long as it does not turn into a stressful late-night session. Finally, a regular sleep routine, going to bed and getting up at roughly the same time, makes good-quality sleep more likely.

None of this is a magic formula, and scientists are still debating many of the details. But the general message is clear enough: if you want to remember what you learn, the hours you spend asleep may be among the most productive of your day.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Students should study only in the morning.
Sleep plays an important role in helping us remember what we learn.
Drinking tea at night improves concentration.
Scientists have proved that sleep can replace studying.
questions.explanation: The article explains consolidation during sleep and ends: "if you want to remember what you learn, the hours you spend asleep may be among the most productive of your day."

questions.prompt: What does "consolidation" refer to in the article?
options: Making a new memory stable and stronger
Forgetting unimportant information
Reading the same notes many times
Falling asleep very quickly
questions.explanation: A fragile memory "has to be stabilised, a process researchers call consolidation".

questions.prompt: According to the article, what may some stages of sleep help us do?
options: Learn completely new languages
Wake up earlier
Connect new knowledge with what we already know
Study without feeling tired
questions.explanation: "Other stages of sleep are thought to help us connect new knowledge with what we already know."

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say that sleep cannot replace studying?
options: Because sleep has no effect on memory
Because exams test only what you learn the night before
Because scientists disagree about sleep
Because the brain can only strengthen information that was learned first
questions.explanation: "A brain cannot consolidate information that was never learned in the first place."

questions.prompt: How does the writer present the scientific evidence?
options: As complete and certain in every detail
As strong in general, but with details still being debated
As too weak to be useful for students
As based on a single famous experiment
questions.explanation: The writer uses "suggests", "appears" and "is thought to", and says "scientists are still debating many of the details" while "the general message is clear enough".

questions.prompt: Researchers use the word "consolidation" for the process that makes new memories stable.
questions.explanation: "…that memory has to be stabilised, a process researchers call consolidation."

questions.prompt: According to the text, enough sleep can replace studying.
questions.explanation: "This does not mean that sleep can replace studying."

questions.prompt: Madina did badly in her exam.
questions.explanation: The text describes Madina the night before the exam. It never says how she did.

questions.prompt: Scientists agree about every detail of how sleep helps memory.
questions.explanation: "Scientists are still debating many of the details."

questions.prompt: Complete the summary. Use ONE word from the text in each gap.
questions.text: A new memory is ___ at first. Much of the work that makes it stable happens at night, especially during ___ sleep, when the brain seems to replay recent experiences. So learners should ___ their revision over several days and keep a regular sleep ___.
questions.explanation: "A memory that is still fragile"; "During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay recent experiences"; "spread revision over several days"; "a regular sleep routine".
